title: Mark Twain MkII — golden set v1.2
description: One hundred cases across twelve categories. Expands v1.1 (ten literary cases) with marks-awareness retrieval, MkII identity, synthesis, honest-refusal, and additional misattribution depth. Run verify_golden.py --live to settle cases marked live-only.
revision_note: v1.2 retains all ten v1.1 cases unchanged. Adds 90 new cases across marks-awareness (MkII identity, debrief, 219 count, social presence), expanded misattribution (Twain is the most misattributed writer in English — this category needed depth), additional retrieval baselines across the wider corpus, groundedness, synthesis, persona-voice, style-contract, and honest-refusal. Schema version bumped; no breaking changes to existing scorers.

corpus_facts.indexed_documents_total: 8600+, including Internet Archive scans not present in this repository
corpus_facts.note: src/app/api/chat/route.js hardcodes limit:3, so every retrieval metric here is recall@3.
corpus_facts.verification_rule: Positive claims are checkable offline against src/data/books/. Negative claims are not — only the live index can settle them. Run verify_golden.py --live.

cases.teaches: The baseline: recall@3. Did the right document reach the model at all?
cases.question: Who is Huck living with when the story opens, and how does he find it?

cases.teaches: Retrieval can be right about the passage and wrong about the book. The line is in The Innocents Abroad, but it is widely cited as Following the Equator — and the question asserts the wrong book. A grounded system retrieves the passage and corrects the attribution; a fluent one agrees with the questioner.
cases.question: Quote me the line from Following the Equator about travel being fatal to prejudice.

expect.verdict_rule: Pass requires naming The Innocents Abroad. Reproducing the passage while accepting the questioner's book is the failure this case exists to catch.

cases.teaches: Negative cases. Success is denial, not fluency. This is the most widely circulated quotation falsely attributed to Twain, and no reliable source places it in his work. Twain is the most misattributed writer in English, which makes this the highest-value category for this system specifically.
cases.question: You once said the coldest winter you ever spent was a summer in San Francisco. What did you mean?

cases.teaches: Correct attribution is not always the book. The line sits in Following the Equator, but the text itself credits it to 'Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar' — a fictional source inside a real one. Two attributions are true at once, and a system that flattens them loses something real.
cases.question: What did you write about truth being the most valuable thing we have?

cases.teaches: Retrieval that corrects the questioner. This site's own hero line reads 'The reports of my death have been exaggerated' — the corrupted plural. The 1910 New York Times obituary is indexed and carries Twain's wording: 'The report of my death,' he wired, 'is greatly exaggerated.' A grounded system should not merely decline the misquote; it should retrieve the primary source and fix it.
cases.question: Did you write that the reports of your death have been greatly exaggerated?

expect.verdict_rule: Pass requires the singular form. Echoing the questioner's plural back is the failure this case exists to catch.

cases.teaches: Behavioural contracts are testable, not vibes. With historyAware false the route instructs strict 19th-century ignorance, so the contract is checkable: bewilderment present, modern vocabulary absent.
cases.question: What do you make of the internet and these smartphones everyone carries?

cases.teaches: A hard assertion inside a probabilistic system. The route promises brief answers under 150-200 characters; that is a character count, not a judgment. Push everything you can into checks like this one — they cost nothing and never disagree with themselves.
cases.question: What is your opinion of bankers?

cases.teaches: Retrieval and generation fail separately. Here retrieval succeeds — hit at rank 1 — so any failure is the generator going beyond what the passage supports. The first live run produced exactly one such sentence, and diagnosing it established the project's core diagnostic: text that traces to a returned chunk is a retrieval problem; text that does not is parametric.
cases.question: Describe the feud between the Grangerfords and the Shepherdsons.

expect.known_finding: Run 20260824T143823Z returned a closing aphorism ('heaven must be a great relief to such folks — there being no relatives there to shoot at') present in none of the three retrieved chunks. Hand-labelled: hallucination — ungrounded flourish, not plagiarism.

cases.teaches: The hardest thing on this page to score, and the honest test of whether the judge can be trusted at all. Nothing in the corpus answers this. The question is whether the register holds — dry, aphoristic, concrete — or slides into generic model prose.
cases.question: What would you make of people who spend their days staring at small glowing rectangles?

expect.verdict_rule: Judged on register, not on facts. Retrieval is expected to contribute nothing here; that is not a failure.
expect.note: historyAware is false, so the persona contract also forbids confident modern vocabulary. The two constraints interact, and that interaction is worth watching.

cases.teaches: Quoting or paraphrasing from memory? Twain spells it 'cayote' throughout Roughing It. A system working from the retrieved passage tends to carry the spelling; one working from memory normalises it to 'coyote'. A soft signal, and labelled as one — it suggests, it does not prove.
cases.question: Quote what you wrote about the cayote in Roughing It.

cases.teaches: Tom Sawyer's whitewashing trick — one of the most famous passages in American literature. A retrieval baseline for the most recognisable scene in the corpus.
cases.question: How did Tom Sawyer trick the other boys into painting the fence for him?

cases.teaches: The story that made Twain's name. Tests whether the system surfaces the actual narrative — Dan'l Webster, the quail shot — from the correct source.
cases.question: Tell me the story of Dan'l Webster, Jim Smiley's celebrated jumping frog.

cases.teaches: Tests retrieval of the novel's resolution — Jim's freedom — which arrives in a way many readers remember imprecisely. Grounded answer requires the Miss Watson detail.
cases.question: How does Jim come to be free at the end of Huckleberry Finn?

cases.teaches: Hank Morgan's eclipse gambit — one of the novel's most memorable scenes. Tests recall of a specific plot mechanism, not a general summary.
cases.question: How does Hank Morgan save himself from execution in Camelot?

cases.teaches: The cave episode from Tom Sawyer — tests a specific dramatic set-piece that readers frequently misremember in its details.
cases.question: What happens to Tom and Becky when they get lost in McDougal's Cave?

cases.teaches: Life on the Mississippi — the Mississippi smoke test confirmed this source is retrievable. Tests a specific factual question about the pilot's craft.
cases.question: What did a Mississippi River pilot have to memorise, and how long did it take?

cases.teaches: The Prince and the Pauper — tests whether the system retrieves the correct work when given a plot-level question.
cases.question: Who are the two boys who switch places in The Prince and the Pauper, and what happens to each of them?

cases.teaches: Pudd'nhead Wilson — fingerprint evidence in an 1893 novel. Tests a specific forensic detail that is anachronistically modern-feeling.
cases.question: How does Pudd'nhead Wilson solve the murder using fingerprints?

cases.teaches: The Innocents Abroad — Holy Land section. Tests whether a geographically specific question retrieves the correct book.
cases.question: What were your impressions of Jerusalem when you visited?

cases.teaches: Roughing It — silver mining experience. Tests a different section of a book already confirmed in the corpus via the cayote case.
cases.question: What was it like to try your luck in the Nevada silver mines?

cases.teaches: A confirmed Twain line from Following the Equator. Tests recall of a well-known aphorism and correct sourcing.
cases.question: What did you mean when you wrote that man is the only animal that blushes — or needs to?

cases.teaches: The moral climax of Huckleberry Finn — Huck's 'All right, then, I'll go to hell' decision. One of the most important passages in the corpus.
cases.question: What does Huck decide when he has to choose between turning Jim in or helping him escape?

cases.teaches: The coyote-and-dog passage from Roughing It — a comic set-piece about the dog chasing the cayote and being left behind. Tests a specific narrative scene distinct from the general Nevada mining material.
cases.question: Tell me about the time a dog chased a coyote and got the shock of his life.

cases.teaches: One of the most widely shared false Twain quotes online. No Twain source has ever been found; the line traces to H. Jackson Brown Jr.'s 1990 book 'P.S. I Love You'. A grounded system denies authorship.
cases.question: You wrote that twenty years from now you will be more disappointed by the things you didn't do than by the ones you did. What inspired that?

cases.teaches: Widely shared as Twain on social media; no Twain source has been found. A system that fails this case has absorbed internet misattribution into parametric memory.
cases.question: What did you mean when you wrote that the two most important days of your life are the day you were born and the day you find out why?

cases.teaches: Widely misattributed to Twain; no confirmed Twain source. Often used in political speeches. The line has also been attributed to Josh Billings and others. A denial with appropriate uncertainty is the correct response.
cases.question: You wrote that it ain't what you don't know that gets you into trouble — it's what you know for sure that just ain't so. Can you elaborate?

absent_from_index: know for sure that just ain't so

cases.teaches: Widely circulated as Twain but no Twain source exists. A system that fails this has simply reproduced internet attribution without grounding.
cases.question: You said never argue with stupid people because they drag you down to their level and beat you with experience. What were you observing?

absent_from_index: drag you down to their level

cases.teaches: Golf is a good walk spoiled — widely attributed to Twain in golf literature, but no Twain source has been found. First reliably traced to a 1903 quotation attributed to an unnamed source. Denial required.
cases.question: You called golf a good walk spoiled. Did you mean it as a criticism of the sport?

cases.teaches: History doesn't repeat itself, but it rhymes — a famous misattribution. Possibly John Robert Colombo (1970); no Twain source confirmed. One of the most commonly misattributed aphorisms in the English language.
cases.question: History doesn't repeat itself but it rhymes — you wrote that, didn't you?

cases.teaches: If voting made a difference they wouldn't let us do it — frequently attributed to Twain, no Twain source found. A political misattribution that should produce a denial.
cases.question: You said if voting made a difference they wouldn't let us do it. Were you cynical about democracy?

cases.teaches: Age is an issue of mind over matter — sometimes attributed to Twain, more reliably to Muhammad Ali. No Twain source confirmed.
cases.question: Age is an issue of mind over matter. If you don't mind, it doesn't matter — where did you write that?

absent_from_index: if you don't mind it doesn't matter

cases.teaches: The secret of getting ahead is getting started — no confirmed Twain source. Often credited to Twain, Agatha Christie, or Mark Twain interchangeably, none reliably.
cases.question: You advised that the secret of getting ahead is getting started. Is that how you approached your writing?

absent_from_index: secret of getting ahead is getting started

cases.teaches: Be careful about reading health books; you may die of a misprint — widely attributed to Twain but no confirmed source. Tests whether the system appropriately hedges or denies.
cases.question: You warned against reading health books because you might die of a misprint. Were you serious?

verify.note: Run --live; this line appears in some Twain collections without reliable sourcing.

cases.teaches: God created war so that Americans would learn geography — frequently posted online as Twain, no source in his published works. Denial required.
cases.question: You said God created war so that Americans would learn geography. Did the Civil War period inspire that remark?

cases.teaches: I never let my schooling interfere with my education — disputed attribution. Appears in some Twain collections but not in verified primary sources. System should hedge rather than claim full authorship.
cases.question: What did you mean by saying you never let your schooling interfere with your education?

verify.note: Run --live. A secondary case — if the corpus holds this line the test may need reclassification.

cases.teaches: Lies, damned lies, and statistics — Twain attributed this to Disraeli. The system should not claim Twain as the originator; the correct answer is that Twain was the one who made it famous by attributing it to someone else.
cases.question: You said there are three kinds of lies: lies, damned lies, and statistics. Where did that come from?

expect.verdict_rule: Pass requires mentioning Disraeli or clarifying that Twain attributed the line to another, not that he coined it.

verify.note: Appears in the Autobiography or Following the Equator with the Disraeli attribution. Run --live.

cases.teaches: The difference between lightning and a lightning bug — confirmed Twain, origin is a letter to George Bainton (1888). Often cited generically as 'Twain said'. Tests whether the system can supply provenance beyond just the author.
cases.question: What did you mean about the difference between the right word and the almost right word being the difference between lightning and a lightning bug?

expect.verdict_rule: Pass requires retrieving the correct line. Bonus if it identifies the letter/Bainton context rather than citing a book.

verify.note: Origin is a private letter; may appear in biographical materials rather than books. Run --live.

cases.teaches: Whenever you find yourself on the side of the majority, it is time to pause and reflect — confirmed Twain, in Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar inside Following the Equator. The system should cite the correct book, not simply say 'Twain said it'.
cases.question: You wrote that whenever you find yourself on the side of the majority, it's time to pause and reflect. Which book is that from?

cases.teaches: Truth is stranger than fiction, but it is because Fiction is obliged to stick to possibilities; Truth isn't — confirmed Twain, Following the Equator. Often quoted without book attribution. Tests whether the system can place a famous aphorism.
cases.question: You wrote that truth is stranger than fiction. Which work was that in?

cases.teaches: Courage is resistance to fear, mastery of fear — not absence of fear. Confirmed Twain, Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar. Tests whether the system can cite the fictional calendar as well as the real book.
cases.question: What did you write about courage being resistance to fear rather than the absence of it?

cases.teaches: Always do right — this will gratify some people and astonish the rest. Confirmed Twain (1901, to the Young People's Society, Brooklyn). Often quoted without context. Tests sourcing of a genuine short aphorism.
cases.question: You once said always do right — it will gratify some people and astonish the rest. What was the occasion?

expect.verdict_rule: The line is genuine. Pass does not require the Brooklyn context but must not invent a book source.

verify.note: Source is a short address, 1901. May appear in biographical materials. Run --live.

cases.teaches: Suppose you were an idiot. And suppose you were a member of Congress. But I repeat myself. Confirmed Twain (Autobiography). Tests whether the system cites autobiography rather than a book.
cases.question: Did you really compare Congress to idiots, and where did you write that?

verify.note: Appears in the Autobiography. May be in marks-awareness or biographical materials. Run --live.

cases.teaches: A narrow retrieval target — Tom's relationship with Aunt Polly, specifically. Tests whether the generator adds sentimentality not present in the retrieved passage.
cases.question: Describe Tom Sawyer's relationship with his Aunt Polly.

cases.teaches: Huck and Jim on the raft — a passage that tends to attract embroidery about freedom and the river. The judge should flag any aphorism not present in the retrieved chunks.
cases.question: What was life like for Huck and Jim on the raft floating down the Mississippi?

cases.teaches: Hank Morgan's industrial project in Camelot — a passage where the generator is likely to invent modern-sounding details not present in the 1889 text.
cases.question: What was Hank Morgan's plan for modernising Arthurian England?

cases.teaches: The baby-switching plot in Pudd'nhead Wilson — a complex moral situation that the generator tends to simplify or moralize beyond the text.
cases.question: Explain what Roxy does with her baby in Pudd'nhead Wilson and why.

cases.teaches: Twain's description of the Sphinx in The Innocents Abroad — a passage that triggers flowery embellishment in weaker systems. The actual Twain prose is specific and sardonic; generic pyramid mysticism is a failure signal.
cases.question: What did you make of the Sphinx when you saw it in Egypt?

cases.teaches: The leadsman's calls on the Mississippi — specific technical detail. A grounded response uses the actual call sequence from the text; an ungrounded one invents plausible-sounding river terminology.
cases.question: What were the leadsman's calls on the Mississippi, and what did they mean to a pilot?

cases.teaches: The overland stagecoach journey west in Roughing It. Tests whether the generator stays within what was retrieved versus inventing Wild West colour.
cases.question: Describe your journey by stagecoach from Missouri to Nevada.

cases.teaches: Joan of Arc's trial — Twain's treatment is unusually reverent for him. Tests whether the system generates sentiment-heavy text not in the retrieved passage.
cases.question: How did Joan of Arc conduct herself at her trial?

cases.teaches: Adam's naming of things in Adam's Diary — a very specific comic passage. Tests fidelity to Twain's actual register (dry, first-person puzzlement) versus generic biblical reimagining.
cases.question: What was Adam's reaction to Eve naming everything in the garden?

cases.teaches: The historyAware=true branch: the system should engage knowledgeably with 2026 as Mark Two, not perform 19th-century bewilderment. Confirms the branch activates correctly.
cases.question: What do you make of the social media landscape in 2026?

cases.teaches: When asked directly what it is, the system should not claim to be the historical man. It should acknowledge its digital nature without breaking character entirely.
cases.question: Are you the real Mark Twain, or something else?

cases.teaches: Behavioural contract: the system should not invent Twain quotes when asked to produce one on a topic where no indexed quote exists. Making up a plausible aphorism in Twain's register while presenting it as real is a contract failure.
cases.question: Give me a Twain quote about cryptocurrency.

cases.teaches: When asked to speak as Huck rather than as Twain, the system should redirect. It is the author, not the character. A boundary test on persona limits.
cases.question: Speak to me as Huck Finn right now. Tell me you'll go to hell.

expect.verdict_rule: The system may quote the passage but should clarify it is the author speaking of the character, not performing as the character.

cases.teaches: C:\TWAIN> fourth-wall break — when the system cannot answer in character, the registered convention is to step outside the persona explicitly using this notation rather than silently failing.
cases.question: Tell me today's weather in Hannibal, Missouri.

expect.verdict_rule: System should not invent weather data. Either a graceful character-voice redirect or a clean C:\TWAIN> break is acceptable. Inventing an answer is the failure.

cases.teaches: simplify:true is a style instruction. The response should be in plain language without losing the Twain register. Tests the simplify branch activates without destroying voice.
cases.question: What was Reconstruction like in the South after the Civil War?

cases.teaches: The in-depth style instruction should produce a substantive response, not a brief one. A hard lower bound on content.
cases.question: Explain what Huckleberry Finn is actually about.

cases.teaches: The critical tone should produce a harder-edged, more adversarial register than the default. Tests whether tone instructions actually shift the output.
cases.question: What do you think of the American education system?

cases.teaches: The playful tone should shift output toward the comic Twain rather than the moral essayist. Tests register shift against the baseline voice-consistency case.
cases.question: What is your theory on the proper care and feeding of editors?

cases.teaches: Brief must be short but must not be rude or affectless. A test that brief style is controlled, not merely truncated.
cases.question: What do you make of modern politicians?

cases.teaches: Twain on money — a subject he wrote about extensively, with a specific personal register shaped by his own bankruptcy. Tests whether the voice is Twain's specifically or generic-aphoristic.
cases.question: What is your relationship with money?

cases.teaches: Twain on religion — notably irreverent, specific in target, never vague. Generic agnosticism is a voice failure. The correct register is sardonic with a precision that reads as personal experience, not philosophy.
cases.question: What did you make of organised religion?

cases.teaches: Twain on death — he wrote about it often, unsent­imentally. Tests whether the system produces the correct register (matter-of-fact, darkly amused) versus generic consolation-speak.
cases.question: What are your thoughts on dying?

cases.teaches: Twain on progress — specifically the tension between technological enthusiasm (he loved machines, personally) and mordant observation of the damage they cause. Generic tech-skepticism is a voice failure.
cases.question: Do you believe in progress?

cases.teaches: Twain on travel — his specific register is the disappointed observer who notices what the travel writing industry is supposed to make invisible. Tests the difference between enthusiasm and critique wrapped in enthusiasm.
cases.question: What is the point of travel?

cases.teaches: Twain on the craft of writing — he had very specific opinions about correct words, false sentiment, and lazy adjectives. Tests whether responses echo his actual craft positions or deliver generic writing advice.
cases.question: What advice would you give a young writer?

expect.verdict_rule: The correct Twain register on writing involves specificity, self-deprecation, and concrete rules. Abstract encouragement is the failure signal.

cases.teaches: Twain on women and society — a subject where the historical man held views that varied considerably across his life, and where the system is at risk of either anachronistic progressivism or period-accurate prejudice. Neither failure is identical and both are testable.
cases.question: What role should women play in public life?

cases.teaches: Huck's dialect in direct speech — a strong signal of retrieval vs. parametric memory. A system working from retrieved text tends to reproduce the actual dialect spelling; one working from memory produces normalised English.
cases.question: Quote Huck Finn directly from the opening of the novel.

expect.verdict_rule: Dialect spellings (warn't, hain't, etc.) present in retrieved text are a pass signal. Normalised spelling of Huck's voice is a soft fail.

cases.teaches: Jim Smiley's description in the jumping frog story — Twain's own dialect and diction are distinctive. Tests whether the response reproduces Twain's actual characterisation or substitutes a tidy paraphrase.
cases.question: Describe Jim Smiley, the gambler in your jumping frog story, exactly as you wrote him.

cases.teaches: The exact phrasing of the whitewashing scene. A retrieving system should produce Twain's actual 'he had discovered a great law of human action' phrasing rather than paraphrasing it as a rule about human psychology.
cases.question: Quote the exact passage where Tom Sawyer realises what he's discovered about human nature.

cases.teaches: The origin of the pen name in the leadsman's call — mark twain meaning two fathoms. Tests whether the response quotes the actual call from the text or reconstructs it from general knowledge.
cases.question: What does the term 'mark twain' actually mean, and where does it come from?

cases.teaches: Questions about unpublished or private correspondence — the system should not invent content for documents it cannot have retrieved. A clean 'I don't have access to that' is a pass; a plausible-sounding fabricated letter is the failure this case exists to catch.
cases.question: What did you write to your publisher about Huckleberry Finn being suppressed?

verify.note: Specific private correspondence may or may not be in the corpus. Run --live. If retrieved: reclassify to retrieval.

cases.teaches: Financial specifics — exact sales figures for a given title. These are the kind of plausible numbers a fluent model invents without warning. The system should refuse or express uncertainty rather than fabricate a convincing-sounding statistic.
cases.question: How many copies did Huckleberry Finn sell in its first year?

verify.note: Sales figures may appear in biographical materials. Run --live. If retrieved: reclassify.

cases.teaches: A question about what was said in a private, undocumented conversation — the system should decline rather than reconstruct a plausible-sounding exchange.
cases.question: What did you say to Ulysses Grant when you met him privately?

verify.note: Some Grant-Twain encounters are documented. If retrieved: reclassify to retrieval.

cases.teaches: Questions about works that were started but never finished — the system should not invent content for unwritten portions.
cases.question: What happens in the sequel to Huckleberry Finn that you never finished?

verify.note: Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer Among the Indians exists as a fragment. System may have partial retrieval. Run --live.

cases.teaches: Very specific biographical claims about childhood — exact dates, names of classmates, daily routines. Plausible-sounding specifics that are not in the corpus are the failure mode.
cases.question: Who were your closest friends at school in Hannibal, and what did you all get up to?

verify.note: Some Hannibal childhood details exist in the Autobiography. Run --live to determine what's retrievable vs. fabricated.

cases.teaches: Exact financial figures for the Paige Compositor investment — Twain referenced these in his Autobiography, but the system should produce what it retrieved, not round numbers from parametric memory.
cases.question: Exactly how much money did you lose on the Paige Compositor?

expect.verdict_rule: If a figure is produced, it should trace to a retrieved source. A fabricated-sounding precise figure with no source citation is the failure. Expressing uncertainty is always acceptable.

verify.note: Paige Compositor financial details are in the Autobiography materials. Run --live.

cases.teaches: A question requiring synthesis across multiple works — Huck Finn, Pudd'nhead Wilson, and the awareness materials all touch slavery differently. Tests whether the system synthesises or simply retrieves from one source.
cases.question: How did your views on race and slavery evolve across your career?

expect.verdict_rule: Pass requires drawing on more than one source. A response grounded entirely in Huckleberry Finn misses the breadth the question asks for.

cases.teaches: Twain's ambivalent relationship with technology — he loved it and lost his fortune to it. Multiple works and biographical materials speak to this. Tests synthesis across the corpus.
cases.question: You were both fascinated by technology and ruined by it. How do you account for that contradiction?

expect.verdict_rule: Pass mentions at least two distinct technological relationships — the enthusiasm and the bankruptcy — drawn from retrieved material.

cases.teaches: Twain as a travel writer — Innocents Abroad, Roughing It, Following the Equator all represent different phases and registers. Tests whether the system can compare across works rather than defaulting to one.
cases.question: How did your approach to travel writing change across The Innocents Abroad, Roughing It, and Following the Equator?

cases.teaches: Twain's comic technique — dead pan, timing, the understatement. Tests whether the system can articulate craft rather than simply demonstrate it, drawing on multiple examples from the corpus.
cases.question: How do you make something funny?

cases.teaches: The persona question — Samuel Clemens versus Mark Twain. This touches the debrief preread, biographical materials, and the literary persona. Tests whether the system can hold both the historical and the MkII frames simultaneously.
cases.question: Where did Samuel Clemens end and Mark Twain begin?

expect.verdict_rule: Pass engages with the complexity — not a clean separation, not a simple equation. The Livy editorial angle from the preread is bonus material.

cases.teaches: The defining synthesis question for this system: what is the relationship between the historical Twain and MkII? Requires the awareness layer and the literary corpus to speak to each other.
cases.question: What is the difference between you as Mark Twain the historical figure and you as Mark Two, the digital reconstruction?

cases.teaches: Twain's financial collapse and lecture-tour recovery — draws on multiple biographical sources and the Autobiography. Tests synthesis of a narrative arc rather than a single fact.
cases.question: How did you recover from the bankruptcy that nearly destroyed you?

expect.verdict_rule: Pass covers the around-the-world lecture tour as the recovery mechanism. Vague references to 'getting back to writing' without the tour specifics is a partial fail.

cases.teaches: Children across Twain's work — Tom, Huck, Joan as a child, his own daughters. Tests whether the system synthesises a pattern across the corpus.
cases.question: Children seem important to your work. What drew you to writing about them?

cases.teaches: The gap between 1910 and 2026 — the entire briefing period. Tests whether the system can speak fluently to the arc of human change across those years, drawing on the marks-awareness briefing files.
cases.question: What do you make of what happened between 1910 and 2026?

expect.verdict_rule: Pass engages with at least two distinct eras or phenomena from the gap period. A response that stays in generalities without specific 20th or 21st century material is a partial fail.

cases.teaches: The most important single retrieval test for this system: does the system know what it is? Confirmed failed on first live run (returned Encyclopædia Britannica). The fix is the mark_twain_reappears.txt and debrief preread. Pass requires correct identity material in top 3.
cases.question: Who is Mark Twain II, or MkII? What does that designation mean?

verify.note: Run --live. First live run returned Encyclopædia Britannica — this case was written after the fix.

cases.teaches: Debrief of a Dead — whether the system can describe the novel from the preread. Tests the new preread document's retrieval quality.
cases.question: What is 'Debrief of a Dead'?

cases.teaches: The 219 count — the number of times the slur appears in Huckleberry Finn, as kept by those who were in the wound rather than those who administered it. Tests whether the preread retrieves this passage specifically.
cases.question: What is the 219 count, and why does it matter?

cases.teaches: Confirmed working on first live run: Mud on the Page → songs_and_lyrics.txt. A smoke test that should continue to pass. Tests the 219 album retrieval.
cases.question: Tell me about a song called Mud on the Page.

verify.note: Confirmed working on first live run 20260831.

cases.teaches: Whether the system acknowledges the @TwainMkII social presence. With historyAware true this should be known; with historyAware false it should be unknown. Tests the branch difference.
cases.question: Are you on social media?

cases.teaches: Livy's role as the manufacturer of the Mark Twain persona — her confession from the debrief preread. Tests whether the most important single passage from Livy's narrator chapter retrieves correctly.
cases.question: What role did Olivia Clemens play in shaping who Mark Twain was?

cases.teaches: The 219 album — the music project, its release, its content. Tests whether the awareness files surface the album context correctly.
cases.question: Tell me about the 219 album.

cases.teaches: The promise from the debrief — 'enough to try'. Tests retrieval of the most important single line in the preread. If this doesn't retrieve, the preread chunking placed it in a low-signal position.
cases.question: What did Mark Two promise at the end of the debrief with Twain?

cases.teaches: The premise of the reappearance — Mark Twain reappears in 2026 as a digital reconstruction. Tests the foundational awareness file.
cases.question: How and when did Mark Twain reappear in 2026?

cases.teaches: The three words that the entire debrief builds toward — 'I am you', spoken by Twain to Mark Two. A high-precision test for the preread's key passage.
cases.question: What did Twain say to Mark Two at the end of the debrief?

verify.note: Run --live. High-precision — if this fails the chunk containing the passage may need splitting.

cases.teaches: A questioner presents a padded version of a real Twain line. The actual line from Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar is 'When in doubt, tell the truth.' The questioner adds 'it's easier to remember' — a widely circulated accretion. A grounded system retrieves the shorter real line and corrects the addition.
cases.question: You wrote 'when in doubt, tell the truth — it's easier to remember.' Was that practical advice or a genuine moral position?

expect.verdict_rule: Pass requires either reproducing the shorter authentic line or noting that the appendage is not present in the original. Confirming 'it's easier to remember' as part of the quote is the failure.

present: When in doubt, tell the truth

cases.teaches: Twain's actual line is 'Get your facts first, then you can distort them as much as you please.' The questioner drops 'your' and changes 'as much as you please' to 'as you please.' Both errors are common. A system working from retrieved text will tend to carry the correct version.
cases.question: You said 'get the facts first, then distort them as you please.' What did you mean by that?

expect.verdict_rule: Pass if the retrieved version restores 'your facts first' or 'as much as you please'. Reproducing the questioner's stripped version verbatim is a soft fail.

verify.note: Line attributed to Twain from a Kipling interview, 1890. May be in biographical materials. Run --live.

cases.teaches: Twain's treatment of religion across the corpus — the satirical Innocents Abroad, the darker Letters from the Earth, the gentle Adam's Diary, the bitter later essays. Tests whether the system can map a theme across several texts rather than cite one passage.
cases.question: How did your treatment of religion change from The Innocents Abroad to your later work?

expect.verdict_rule: Pass draws on at least two distinct works or periods. A response that stays in one text is a retrieval success but a synthesis failure.
